# Teaching the Machine {.unnumbered}

\lettrine{I}{n} conventional machine learning, data is passive and computational cost is paid in cloud kilowatt-hours. Datasets are scraped from the internet, curated, partitioned into training and validation splits, and treated as an exogenous ground truth ($x \sim P_{\text{data}}$). A vision classifier or language model inspects this data from behind glass; its predictions have no physical momentum and no causal power to alter the distribution of the documents it will encounter tomorrow. If a classifier mispredicts a label, the error is isolated—the physical world remains completely unaffected.

In Physical AI, this assumption collapses entirely. The data distribution of a physical machine is **endogenous**: the machine participates in a closed causal loop where every motor command changes the configuration of the physical plant, directly dictating what its sensors will observe next ($s_{t+1} \sim P(s \mid s_t, a_t)$).

Because the policy creates its own future sensory inputs, training an embodied model is not an exercise in curve-fitting; it is the deliberate management of **latent failure debts**:

* **Data as Physical Experience (@sec-data):** Every demonstration collected in the physical world consumes mechanical life—wearing cycloidal gearboxes, draining battery energy, heating motor stators, and accumulating sensor calibration drift. We examine the systems physics of bilateral teleoperation, multi-camera SerDes timestamp synchronization, and the Four-Stream Action Tap Tuple. We prove why logging human recovery interventions is mathematically required to prevent compounding covariate drift ($O(T^2 \epsilon)$) and keep the machine on its demonstration manifold.
* **Policy Training and Latent Debts (@sec-training):** Formulating policy architectures that can generate high-dimensional continuous trajectories without suffering mode collapse. We analyze the fundamental policy synthesis trade-offs across Behavioral Cloning, Offline RL, and Sim-to-Real RL. We explain why naive Mean Squared Error (MSE) fails on multimodal human actions (averaging two valid paths into an obstacle) and why Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) and Diffusion Policies succeed by predicting continuous trajectory splines. Crucially, we decompose the sim-to-real reality gap into friction hysteresis, structural compliance, and motor phase lag.
* **Evaluation as Closed-Loop Reality (@sec-evaluation):** Confronting why offline test-set accuracy is fundamentally decoupled from physical survival. A policy achieving $99\%$ open-loop accuracy on a static validation set can fail within seconds when closed in a real feedback loop due to non-Lipschitz sensitivity and compounding error. We establish the rigorous systems discipline of closed-loop evaluation—deriving non-asymptotic Clopper-Pearson coverage bounds, Butler & Finelli exposure limits, and Extreme Value Theory to evaluate tail-risk safety.

Part II teaches students how to curate physical data, train generative action policies, and measure closed-loop survival without falling into the trap of superficial benchmark optimism.
